newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Iraqi health system near collapse, WHO says.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi health system near collapse, WHO says.

text.p: Iraq's health system is close to collapse and medicines and other life-saving supplies scheduled for importation under the "oil-for-food" deal have failed to arrive, the World Health Organisation (WHO) said on Thursday.
A spokesman said the United Nations health agency was working with the U.N. Sanctions Committee in New York to speed up its processing of Iraqi contracts with medical suppliers.

The deal, which took effect last December, allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over six months partly to buy food and medicine for its more than 20 million people suffering from sanctions imposed by the U.N. after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.

But WHO expressed concern that diseases, including malaria and typhoid threatened to reappear in large parts of Iraq. Hospitals lacked basic medicines and electricity to refrigerate vaccines against deadly outbreaks of polio and diptheria.
WHO director-general Hiroshi Nakajima and four experts made a four-day trip to Iraq which ended on Monday.
Nakajima, a Japanese pharmacologist, visited hospitals in Najaf and Kerbela, two clinics in sprawling suburbs of Baghdad and a health facility in Babil, according to officials.
"Government drug warehouses and pharmacies have few stocks of medicines and medical supplies," WHO said in a statement.

Nakajima was quoted as saying: "The consequences of this situation are causing a near breakdown of the health care system, which is reeling under the pressure of being deprived of medicine, other basic supplies and spare parts."

Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf, speaking in New York on Wednesday after discussing ways to accelerate the deal with the president of the Security Council, told reporters: "Any practical person will see that up to now not one gram of food or medicine has reached Iraq."

Iraqi Health Minister Umeed Madhat Mubarak, in an interview with Reuters Television on February 18, accused the Sanctions Committee of delaying arrival of medical imports. At the time, he said the U.N. had approved only one contract of 347 submitted.
Nakajima met Vice-President Taha Yassin Ramadan, Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz and Mubarak, officials said.

"He was there to look at implementation of Security Council resolution 986. There is a problem in the delivery and arrival of medicines. WHO will work with New York to speed up processing of contracts," spokesman Richard LeClair said.
Kio Akasaka, an aide who accompanied Nakajima, told Reuters: "We were already aware of the worsening health situation.
"No medicine or medical supplies have arrived yet in the country. Some is due to arrive very soon," he added. "We believe the Sanctions Committee is doing its best."
In most of the country, WHO has an "observer" role to ensure equitable distribution of health products worth $210 million to be imported into Iraq during the six-month period.
WHO is also charged with directly distributing $28.8 million worth of medicines and medical supplies in the three northern governorates where Kurds are under international protection.
Joseph Hazbun, a WHO official, was on Nakajima's mission and remains in northern Iraq to check on distribution plans.
WHO plans to employ 20 international staff, backed by 100 local staff, to observe government distribution in most of the country and carry out distribution in the north, Akasaka said.
